Engraulis anchoita, the Argentine anchoita, reaches an ultimate standard length of 17 centimeters [Li = 17 centimeters], a size that distinguishes it from several smaller congeners in the southwestern Atlantic. Juveniles begin maturing when they attain a standard length at puberty of approximately 9 centimeters [Lp = approximately 9 centimeters], though field surveys indicate this value can range from 8 to 10.2 centimeters depending on local environmental conditions. The onset of gonadal recrudescence is closely linked to thermal regimes; under a stable water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], the maximum reproductive rate translates to roughly 2.2 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 2.2 eggs per day], typically expressed through multiple spawning events during the extended breeding season. Detailed ichthyoplankton surveys reveal that the pelagic eggs, with a mean diameter of 1.2 millimeters, produce hatchlings with a dry weight at birth of 0.0009 grams [Wwb = 0.0009 grams], reflecting the modest yolk reserves characteristic of small clupeiform embryos. This remarkably low initial mass imposes a narrow window for first exogenous feeding, as the yolk-sac larva must rapidly develop the mouth gape and retinal differentiation necessary to capture planktonic prey before endogenous reserves are fully exhausted.

Hatching dynamics in this species are strongly temperature-dependent, with the incubation period for the transparent, pelagic egg lasting only 6 days [ab = 6 days] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a value derived from comparative data on the congener Engraulis encrasicolus. At this thermal condition, chorion rupture and yolk-sac larva emergence occur synchronously, and the newly hatched prolarvae display a pronounced dependence on their endogenous yolk supply. The temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] is notably higher than the 8 °C [T = 8 °C] regime under which maximum longevity has been assessed in captive studies. Across the broader distribution of Argentine anchoita, spawning activity peaks during the austral spring and summer when surface waters commonly reach 15 °C [T = 15 °C], thereby ensuring rapid embryonic development and high survival probabilities for the exogenously feeding larva. This interplay between temperature and early ontogeny is critical for recruitment success, as mismatches between hatching phenology and prey availability can lead to substantial larval mortality during the trophic switch to active feeding.

The asymptotic adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, of Engraulis anchoita has been estimated at 50.5 grams [Wwi = 50.5 grams] based on morphometric regressions relating standard length to total mass in mature individuals. This value corresponds to a fusiform body plan that facilitates efficient filter-feeding on zooplankton in the productive waters of the Argentine shelf. Spawning adults exhibit an iteroparous strategy, with females producing multiple batches of pelagic eggs across the breeding season. Under the cool thermal conditions of 8 °C [T = 8 °C] that prevail in much of their wintering habitat, spawning events are less frequent, but the total annual egg output remains considerable. Gravid individuals sampled during peak reproductive months typically carry developing oocytes at various stages of vitellogenesis, reflecting a batch-spawning mode that spreads reproductive risk across the season. The ultimate wet weight of 50.5 grams is not always attained in all populations; some sub-adult and older individuals in less productive sectors of the shelf may plateau at a lower mass, indicating density-dependent regulation of growth trajectories.

Longevity records for Argentine anchoita, based on otolith increment analysis and mark-recapture studies of the closely related European anchovy Engraulis encrasicolus, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] under a thermal regime of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. This lifespan of about 1,825 days [am = about 1,825 days] at the same water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C] places Engraulis anchoita among the shorter-lived members of the family Engraulidae, a pattern consistent with its relatively rapid maturation and high natural mortality rate. Age-related mortality increases markedly after the fourth year, with very few individuals surviving to the fifth annual spawning season. The longevity estimate of 5 years [am = 5 years] at 8 °C [T = 8 °C] stands in contrast to the faster developmental pace observed at warmer temperatures: embryonic development, for instance, is completed in just 6 days [ab = 6 days] when incubation occurs at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This thermal sensitivity of life-history traits underscores the importance of water temperature as a key environmental driver for population dynamics in the southwestern Atlantic.

In comparative physiological perspective, the Argentine anchoita's life-history syndrome is shaped by the cool, productive waters it inhabits. The ultimate standard length of 17 centimeters [Li = 17 centimeters] and the standard length at puberty of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters] together indicate that approximately half of the maximum body length is achieved before the onset of reproductive maturity, a common pattern among short-lived, batch-spawning clupeiforms. The extreme lightness of the hatchlings, with a dry weight at birth of 0.0009 grams [Wwb = 0.0009 grams], is consistent with the small egg diameter of 1.2 millimeters and the limited per-offspring investment typical of pelagic spawners. At the opposite end of the size spectrum, the ultimate wet weight of 50.5 grams [Wwi = 50.5 grams] sets an upper boundary on somatic growth that constrains the maximum reproductive rate observed at 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. Future field studies could usefully examine whether the 6-day incubation period (6 days) [ab = 6 days] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] shifts significantly under variable thermal regimes, and whether the 5-year lifespan (5 years) [am = 5 years] at 8 °C [T = 8 °C] is extended at cooler temperatures near the southern limit of the species range.
